Address the device answers on. Its own, not a guess: a device that has to be hunted for is found by rate and framing, never by walking addresses.
Function code for the probe read. 3 for holding registers, 4 for input.
Register to read as the probe. Any register that always answers will do - the reply is never decoded, it only has to arrive.

Function code for the correction. 6 for a single holding register.
Register holding the setting that has to change - the device's baud rate, in the only case that exists so far.
Value that puts the device on this bus. The device encodes it, because only the device knows whether its register takes a rate, a code or an index.
Rates to try, in the order worth trying them, and how many of them are filled. Put the bus rate first: a device that is already commissioned then costs one Modbus exchange and the sweep ends there.
Framing codes to try, same idea. 255 means leave the port's own framing, which is the ordinary case; 1..3 force the raw SysCom code, because the enumerator names are not portable across runtimes.
Topic suffix for the retained result, under the bus prefix. Empty publishes nothing.
Modbus unit id of the slave this step addresses.
3 read holding, 4 read input, 6 write single, 16 write multiple. Anything else is rejected by the transport rather than guessed at.
First register, read or write. One field, because a step is only ever one or the other.
Registers to read, or to write. Ignored by FC6, which is always one.
Payload for a write step. Eight registers is the most an FC16 frame may carry here, which bounds the transmit buffer at 9 + 2*8 = 25 bytes.

TRUE skips the remaining steps of the transaction if this one fails. Set it on the write of a read-after-write: publishing a read-back that never happened, after a write that failed, is the exact inaccuracy the pairing exists to remove.
FALSE - the default - suits a batch of independent reads, where one failing register block should not cost the others.

A reply arrived, addressed to us, with the function code we asked for and a CRC of zero over the whole trimmed frame. For a read, ReadBuffer holds Registers() words.

No reply, a bad CRC, the wrong slave, the wrong function code, or a Modbus exception reply. Which of those it was is in the transport's counters, not in this value - the scheduler does not need to care and the counters are how a line fault is diagnosed without a scope.
Nothing to do. The scheduler passes over this device.
A routine read whose interval timer has elapsed. Served round-robin, after every pending COMMAND.

documentation.xhtml: Manual up, e.g. straight from a pushbutton's long-press output. Held TRUE drives the motor up and releasing it stops and holds where it is, which is what a physical button should do - the position it was travelling to is abandoned rather than resumed.
Manual down, same contract as UP. Both at once is not a command and is ignored, because there is no sane guess to make.

Nothing may drive the motor while this is TRUE - a wind alarm, a service switch, an open window contact. Commands are still accepted and still remembered; they simply do not move anything until it clears.

How long the cover takes to travel from fully closed to fully open, and back. These two are how the position is known at all: there is no encoder on a shutter motor, so run time is integrated against them.
Measure them rather than guessing, and measure both - a shutter usually falls faster than it climbs. Being 10% out shows up as a position that drifts from reality in the middle of the travel and snaps back at the end stops, where it recalibrates.
Dead time between a stop and starting the other direction, so a reversing contactor is never asked to change its mind while the motor is still turning.

How long to keep the motor running once an end stop is reached. This is what keeps the estimate honest: every full journey ends against the stop, so the position is measured there rather than integrated forever.
How close to the requested position counts as arrived, in percent. Below about 2 the cover hunts, because a shutter cannot be positioned finer than its own start and stop time.

Percent of travel between position publishes while the cover is moving. Every step is one MQTT message; 5 gives a slider that visibly moves without putting twenty messages on the broker per journey. The exact position is always published once movement ends, whatever this is set to.
Motor contactors. Never both TRUE, and never switched straight from one to the other - T_Lockout always passes between them.
How far open, 0 closed to 100 open, the way Home Assistant counts a cover.
A motor is running.
An end stop has been reached since power-up, so the position is measured rather than assumed. FALSE means the cover has not yet been anywhere it could be sure of.

Where the cover has been asked to go, in percent. Zero at power-up, which together with Arrived means "stay put" rather than "close" - see below.

The current target has been satisfied, so nothing should move until something asks again. A single-producer / single-consumer ring buffer.
EMPTY and FULL used to be stored BOOL outputs, written by both sides, and that was the whole problem. With pw = pr the ring is either completely empty or completely full, and only those two flags told the cases apart - so a task that lost a race on them could leave a non-empty queue looking empty (the workers stop draining, and a retained state change sits unsent until the next publish), or clear FULL while the ring really was full (a writer then overruns entries the reader has not taken yet).
They are derived now. HasMessage() is pr <> pw; IsFull() is INC1(pw,n) = pr. Nothing shared is mutable any more: pw is written only by AddMessage, pr only by GetMessage, and each side merely reads the other's index - a single aligned INT load on this 32-bit target, which cannot tear. No semaphore, so no priority inversion on MainTask or HvacTask.
The cost is exactly one slot. Reporting full one slot early is what buys pw = pr its unambiguous "empty" meaning, so capacity is n rather than n+1.
What this does NOT fix: two tasks inside AddMessage at the same time can still read the same pw, leave one hybrid message in that slot and the next slot never written at all. Only one queue per producer fixes that.

Arbitrates one RS485 bus between the devices registered on it.
The unit of arbitration is a TRANSACTION: an ordered list of steps that a device hands over in one go, executed back to back with the bus held throughout. That is what makes a write and its read-back inseparable - no other device's traffic can land between them - and it is why a meter with three register blocks now wins the bus once per poll round instead of three times.
Selection resumes at a cursor rather than restarting at device 0, so the device registered last is served as often as the device registered first. The old loop ran FOR 0 TO count-1 and took the first taker, which is strict priority by registration order dressed up as a scan.
Commands are looked for before polls, each pass round-robin from the same cursor, so a Home Assistant command does not queue behind every meter while a chatty device still cannot starve a quiet one.
The protocol lives behind RS485Transport. This block never sees a CRC, a function code or a serial handle.

ST.xhtml:
(* Round-robin from the cursor, twice: once for work somebody is waiting on, once for routine polling.
Starting each pass at Cursor rather than at 0 is the whole fairness story. The loop this replaces ran FOR 0 TO devicesCount - 1 and EXITed on the first taker, so device 0 won every contested cycle and the device registered last only ever got the bus when everything above it was idle. With two meters on five-second polls that is invisible; with thirty nodes it is starvation.
Both passes sweep every device, so a COMMAND anywhere beats a POLL everywhere - but COMMANDs are themselves served round-robin, so a chatty device cannot monopolise the bus either. *)
SelectNext := -1;
FOR k := 0 TO devicesCount - 1 DO i := (Cursor + k) MOD devicesCount; IF devices[i].HasWork() = RS485_WorkLevel.COMMAND THEN SelectNext := i; RETURN; END_IF END_FOR
FOR k := 0 TO devicesCount - 1 DO i := (Cursor + k) MOD devicesCount; IF devices[i].HasWork() = RS485_WorkLevel.POLL THEN SelectNext := i; RETURN; END_IF END_FOR

Availability is a judgement, not a reading. One missed reply on a shared RS485 bus is ordinary - a slave that was mid-measurement, a collision with another device's turnaround - and publishing 'offline' on the strength of it makes the Home Assistant connectivity sensor flap between states that are both wrong. So failures have to accumulate before the device is declared down, and recovery is immediate on the first good transaction: being slow to trust and quick to forgive is the right asymmetry when the cost of a false 'offline' is an entity that looks broken.

Modbus RTU master for the PFC's onboard serial port, behind RS485Transport.
This is the code that was proven on the bench in #182, lifted out of the RS485_RUN action into a block of its own and taught the write function codes it was missing. Two things about this hardware are baked in and deliberate:
- Every reply arrives wrapped in glitch bytes - one 00 as the slave's driver enables, another as it releases, because the pair is undriven between frames. Measured across 34 consecutive captures: 34 leading nulls, 34 trailing nulls, 34 CRC-valid frames once trimmed. So the frame is trimmed and the CRC judges what is left, rather than the first byte being trusted.
- The frame is delimited by silence, which is what RTU actually specifies, not by a byte count read out of the header.

ST.xhtml: ReadBuffer := ADR(Data);

(* Find the frame inside what has been collected. Sets `first` and `last`, and returns whether the bytes between them check out.
Counts nothing, changes no state beyond those two indices, and is safe to call every cycle - which is the point. Service uses it to notice that a frame is already complete instead of waiting out the silence, and Judge uses it to decide what it is looking at.
This RESYNCHRONISES rather than merely trimming a leading run of nulls, and that distinction is the whole reason it was rewritten. Trimming nulls handles the driver-enable glitch this hardware produces, and nothing else: put any non-zero byte in front of the reply and every CRC trial fails, because the window always started at that byte. Measured on a DFRobot SEN0492, one reply in three was being thrown away that way - bytes present, LeadNulls climbing, CrcFail climbing, and the sensor answering perfectly well the whole time.
Three things put a non-zero byte in front of a reply, and all of them are ordinary rather than exotic: - a slave that echoes the request before answering, which is documented behaviour for the SEN0492 and reported for others; - a byte left over from the previous exchange that arrived after Start flushed the port; - two replies collected into one window, when a slave answers late enough to land inside the next poll. All three are cured by asking "does a valid frame start HERE?" at every plausible offset instead of assuming the answer is offset zero.
The search is anchored on the slave address rather than sweeping blindly, which keeps the number of CRC trials small and, more importantly, keeps the chance of a coincidental CRC match negligible. *) Frame := FALSE; first := 0;
WHILE NOT Frame AND first <= (count - 5) DO
(* Only a byte that could be this slave's reply is worth testing. *) IF Rx[first] = Step.DeviceId THEN
(* Trailing bytes are removed by asking the CRC rather than by assuming a trailing 00 is noise. It usually is - but a frame whose CRC high byte is genuinely 00 turns up about once in 256, and blindly trimming it turned a perfectly good reply into a CRC failure. *) last := count; tries := 0;
WHILE NOT Frame AND tries < 4 AND (last - first) >= 5 DO IF THIS^.Crc16(pBuf := ADR(Rx[first]), Len := last - first) = 0 THEN Frame := TRUE; ELSE last := last - 1; tries := tries + 1; END_IF END_WHILE
END_IF
IF NOT Frame THEN first := first + 1; END_IF
END_WHILE
(* Nothing framed. Leave `first` and `last` describing the buffer the way the old null-trimming did, because Judge classifies the failure from them: a `first` left pointing near the end would turn a CRC failure into a reported short frame, which is a worse diagnosis than the one it replaces. *) IF NOT Frame THEN first := 0; WHILE first < count AND Rx[first] = 0 DO first := first + 1; END_WHILE last := count; END_IF

(* Close and re-open on the next Service. Clears PortError too, so a port that failed to open at boot - a controller still coming up, say - can be retried without a download. *) ReopenRequest := TRUE;

Asked once at startup by whatever runs commissioning, never by the scheduler, and before any polling has happened. Return FALSE - which is the ordinary case, and what a device configured by switches or by its own display should return - and nothing happens.
Return TRUE and fill pRequest^ to have the bus swept for this device and the register named there written. The device supplies all of it: the address to probe, the register that holds the setting, the value that puts it on this bus, and the rates worth trying. Nothing outside the device has to know what kind of device it is.
BusBaudrate is what the bus itself runs at, passed in so a device can encode that rate the way its own register expects, and can withdraw if it cannot be told to use it.
How many words of ReadBuffer the last OK step filled. Zero after a write.
Where a read step's registers landed. Valid only in the cycle Service returns OK.

Call every cycle. Drives the transport's own state machine and reports where the current step has got to. OK and FAILED are each reported for exactly one cycle, after which the transport returns to IDLE and will accept another Start.

Begin one exchange. Returns FALSE and does nothing if the port is not open, if a step is already in flight, or if the function code is not one this transport implements - an unsupported code is refused rather than framed as a guess.
0 keeps the configured rate
255 keeps the configured framing
T#0S keeps the configured timeout
T#0S keeps the configured gap

Re-open the bus at a different setting, keeping everything Init configured that is not named here.
Sentinels rather than optional parameters, because a caller sweeping a bus needs to vary one field at a time: 0 for a rate or a time and 255 for framing all mean "leave it alone".
This is what makes commissioning possible at all - a device that ships on the wrong baud rate has to be hunted for at rates the bus does not use - and it belongs here rather than at the caller: nothing outside can see the port settings, and nothing outside should have to know the port, parity or buffer size in order to change one field.
Returns FALSE from a transport that cannot be re-tuned. A sweep must then give up rather than probe at a setting it only thinks it applied.

Put the bus back to exactly what Init configured, however far a sweep wandered.
Kept as the transport's own saved copy rather than re-derived, so a caller does not have to remember what it passed to Init in order to hand it back - and so a sweep that ends early, or fails, still leaves a bus the rest of the devices can use.

Bytes in the last receive window, framed or not.
The counter that matters when a device answers nothing at all. Zero bytes at every setting is a bus with nothing on it; bytes that arrive and never frame are a device that is present and being read wrongly - or a pair that is the wrong way round. That distinction is invisible from anywhere else, and it is the one that says whether to keep sweeping settings or go and look at the wiring.
